content:
Your church's federal income-tax exemption does not make a minister's pay tax-free. A minister can be an employee for income-tax purposes while paying self-employment tax on ministerial earnings.

Use this reference to separate the church's tax questions from your own before reviewing compensation and reimbursements with a CPA familiar with clergy tax rules. It summarizes U.S. federal rules; it does not resolve individual tax situations.

---

## Start with the church's exemption

A church that meets section 501(c)(3) requirements is automatically exempt from federal income tax and does not have to apply for IRS recognition. The exemption depends on meeting those requirements, whether or not the church obtains a determination letter.

The church must be organized and operated exclusively for qualifying exempt purposes. It cannot distribute net earnings for private benefit or intervene in political campaigns. No substantial part of its activity may be attempting to influence legislation. Its purposes and activities also cannot be illegal or violate fundamental public policy.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance checked October 15, 2026. This reference uses IRS Publication 1828, revised August 2015, and Publication 517 for 2025 returns. Confirm current forms, thresholds, payment dates and any later changes with the IRS before acting.
</Callout>

---

## Know which filings can still apply

Churches are generally not required to file Form 990, Form 990-EZ or Form 990-N. That exception does not eliminate employment-tax obligations or a return for unrelated business income.

Unrelated business income generally comes from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and is not substantially related to the church's exempt purpose. Using the money for ministry does not, by itself, make the activity related. Exceptions exist, including certain activities where substantially all the work is performed by volunteers, so review the activity before deciding its tax treatment.

A church with $1,000 or more in gross income from an unrelated trade or business during a taxable year must file Form 990-T. The filing test uses gross income, not the activity's profit.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Render to all what is due them: tax to whom tax is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor."* — Romans 13:7 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Distinguish employment from ministerial tax treatment

The IRS clergy rules refer to duly ordained, commissioned or licensed ministers and services performed in the exercise of ministry. Review those qualifications and the work being paid for before applying ministerial treatment.

If a congregation employs you and pays you a salary, you are generally an employee with wages for income-tax purposes. The church reports an employee minister's compensation on Form W-2. Self-employment tax treatment does not, by itself, make you an independent contractor.

Ministerial earnings are generally subject to Social Security and Medicare under the Self-Employment Contributions Act, or SECA, rather than payroll FICA. An applicable IRS-approved exemption can change that treatment. Do not assume the church's income-tax exemption is a personal exemption from SECA.

---

## Designate a housing allowance before payment

If your compensation includes a qualifying housing allowance, the employing church must officially designate a definite amount before paying it. It cannot determine the amount afterward. If no amount has been officially designated, the full salary is included in income.

An employment contract, church minutes, a budget or another official action taken before payment may show the designation. If a local congregation employs and pays you, that congregation must designate the allowance; a national church agency's resolution does not substitute for its action.

---

## Apply the housing exclusion limits

For a minister who owns a home, the income-tax exclusion is limited to the smallest of the following amounts:

- The amount actually used to provide a home.
- The amount officially designated as a housing allowance.
- The home's fair rental value, including furnishings and utilities.

The allowance must also stay within reasonable pay for your services. If the church provides a parsonage as part of your pay, you can exclude its fair rental value, including utilities, from income tax, up to reasonable pay for your services. Include any excess rental allowance in gross income.

<Callout type="warning">
The housing exclusion is for income tax. For a minister in active ministry subject to SECA, the housing allowance or parsonage value is included when figuring net earnings from self-employment. An official designation alone does not make the payment free of all federal taxes.
</Callout>

---

## Plan how personal taxes will be paid

A duly ordained, commissioned or licensed minister's salary for ministerial services is not subject to mandatory federal income-tax withholding. A minister who is a common-law employee can agree with the church to voluntary withholding to cover income tax and self-employment tax.

Without withholding, or with too little withheld, estimated tax payments may be needed. Review the payment arrangement with your CPA instead of treating the absence of mandatory withholding as an absence of tax.

---

## Keep reimbursements separate from compensation

An accountable reimbursement plan must have a business connection, require adequate expense accounting, and require the employee to return excess reimbursements. Both the accounting and the return of excess amounts must happen within a reasonable period.

Provide enough detail to identify the business nature of each expense and substantiate it. Broad labels such as "miscellaneous business expenses" are not sufficient. Qualifying accountable-plan reimbursements are excluded from income and are not reported on Form W-2.

Payments under a nonaccountable plan are included with wages or other compensation on Form W-2. For employee ministers, that reporting does not itself create mandatory federal income-tax withholding or FICA on ministerial compensation.

---

## Prepare for your tax review

Use these questions to review the records behind the tax treatment:

- [ ] Has the church reviewed which employment and unrelated-business returns apply?
- [ ] Does the minister's employment reporting agree with the work arrangement?
- [ ] Was the definite housing allowance officially designated before payment?
- [ ] Do actual housing costs and fair rental value support the exclusion?
- [ ] Is voluntary withholding or an estimated-payment plan in place where needed?
- [ ] Do reimbursements meet the accountable-plan requirements?

<Callout type="tip">
Have a CPA familiar with Publication 517 review the minister's tax treatment, housing allowance and reimbursements before you rely on them. Publication 517 reminds you that you remain responsible for the accuracy of every item reported on your return, even when a paid preparer signs it.
</Callout>

sources.claim: Provide enough detail to identify the business nature of each expense and substantiate it. Broad labels such as "miscellaneous business expenses" are not sufficient. Qualifying accountable-plan reimbursements are excluded from income and are not reported on Form W-2.
sources.quote: Employee business expenses reimbursed under an accountable plan are: (a) excluded from an employee’s gross income, (b) not required to be reported on the 24 employee’s IRS Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement, and (c) exempt from the with- holding and payment of wages subject to FICA taxes and income tax withholdings.

sources.claim: Payments under a nonaccountable plan are included with wages or other compensation on Form W-2. For employee ministers, that reporting does not itself create mandatory federal income-tax withholding or FICA on ministerial compensation.
sources.quote: Your employer will combine any reimbursement paid to you under a nonaccountable plan with your wages, salary, or other compensation and report the combined total in box 1 of your Form W-2.

sources.claim: Payments under a nonaccountable plan are included with wages or other compensation on Form W-2. For employee ministers, that reporting does not itself create mandatory federal income-tax withholding or FICA on ministerial compensation.
sources.quote: If the church or religious organization reimburses or advances the employee for business expenses, but the arrangement does not satisfy the three requirements of an accountable plan, the amounts paid to the employees are considered wages subject to FICA taxes and income tax withholding, if applicable, and are reportable on Form W-2. (Amounts paid to employee ministers are treated as wages reportable on Form W-2, but are not subject to FICA taxes or income tax withholding.)

sources.claim:
<Callout type="tip">
Choose your tax preparer carefully and provide all information needed for an accurate return. Publication 517 reminds you that you remain responsible for the accuracy of every item reported, even when a preparer signs the return.
</Callout>
sources.quote: Although the tax preparer always signs the return, you’re ultimately responsible for providing all the information required for the preparer to accurately prepare your return and for the accuracy of every item reported on the return.

Resolved overlap: retain the published payroll article's employee/SECA distinction and advance housing designation; leave hiring forms, payroll deposits, employer record-retention periods and wage-statement deadlines in that article.
Resolved wording: the $1,000 Form 990-T test is gross unrelated-business income of $1,000 or more for a taxable year, not profit or more than $1,000.
Resolved scope: the housing SECA statement is limited to active ministry subject to SECA; retirement and other specialized exceptions are not summarized.
